chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ayyub ibn Nuhr from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār from one who narrated to him from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) who said:

A woman came to ʿUmar asking him about her divorce. He said, 'Go to this man and ask him,' meaning ʿAlī (peace be upon him). She said to ʿAlī (peace be upon him), 'My husband has divorced me.' He said, 'Did you wash your private part?' She returned to ʿUmar and said, 'He sent me to a man who plays (makes fun).' He said, 'So he sent her back to him twice; every time she returned she said, 'He plays.' He said, 'So he said to her, 'Go to him, for he is the most knowledgeable of us.' He said, 'So ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said to her, 'Did you wash your private part?' She said, 'No.' He said, 'Then your husband has more right to your private part as long as you have not washed your private part.' These two reports and what has come in their meaning do not contradict the preceding reports, because the reason is that it was a case of precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah) or attributing the opinion to them. Thus, the statement of Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) saying, 'ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said,
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a woman's divorce if she has not washed her private part, and how is the apparent contradiction with other narrations resolved?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the jurisprudential nuance in the ruling of *rajʿi* (retractable) divorce, where Imam ʿAlī’s inquiry about washing the private part (*ghusl*) determined whether the husband retained conjugal rights. The scholar contextualizes this by suggesting the ruling may have been an act of *taqiyyah* or a reflection of the opposing sect's view, a perspective corroborated by Imam Abū Jaʿfar’s assertion that the opponents fabricated the specific stance. This highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling apparent contradictions by distinguishing between practical legal rulings and doctrinal truth.
